extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of experimental physics and physical sciences; experimentalists learning measurement theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, conducting, and interpreting quantitative physical measurements: choosing units, using dimensional analysis, classifying constants, and methods to disentangle and eliminate interfering effects and errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of provisional units
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional unit is 'one which is assumed and physically defined in a safe and reproducible manner' so that particular quantities may be compared relatively until absolute relations to primary units are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a conveniently reproducible physical standard (example: the Bunsen and Roscoe light standard) rather than delaying all measurement until absolute energy relations are determined; provisional units enable continued progress while exact relations (e.g., energy content of light) are later investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose units that reflect the underlying physical quantity (heat as energy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit of heat 'ought to be simply the unit of energy,' but in practice a provisional unit is accepted (often the heat required to raise one gram of water through 1°C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physically meaningful provisional definitions (e.g., calorimetric or latent-heat definitions), and where possible relate them approximately to mass, length, time via constants like Joule's mechanical equivalent; alternative definitions (e.g., amount of ice melted at 0°C) are also valid operational standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Dimensions (derived units depend on fundamental units)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derived units are expressed in terms of fundamental units (denote length by L, time by T, mass by M, density by D); e.g., area L^2, volume L^3, velocity L T^-1, acceleration L T^-2, momentum M L T^-1, force M L T^-2, work M L^2 T^-2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally denote dimensions and use them to trace how each derived quantity depends on fundamental units; substitute provisional symbols (M, L, T) where convenient; consult standard references (Everett, Maxwell, Jenkin) for systematic tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angular magnitude is dimensionless
rubrics_metrics.description: Angular magnitude has no dimensions because it is the ratio of arc to radius; pure numerical functions (sines, logarithms, exponents) are likewise devoid of dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat angles as dimensionless in dimensional expressions, but remember that derived angular quantities (angular velocity, angular acceleration) acquire time dimensions (e.g., angular velocity T^-1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Homogeneity (dimensional consistency test)
rubrics_metrics.description: All quantities added together or equated in any equation must have the same dimensions; if terms are not homogeneous some blunder has been committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dimensional homogeneity as an infallible check on mathematical reasoning: non-homogeneous equations (e.g., adding force to velocity) reveal errors that changing units would expose; apply routinely during derivations and error checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dimensions to deduce numerical changes under unit changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When fundamental units are changed, numerical expressions of derived quantities vary according to their dimensional exponents: inversely as the magnitude of the unit for each positive whole dimension and directly for negative dimensions; fractional exponents require taking the appropriate root of the ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the rule to convert numbers (example: yard to foot, foot to inch) and to determine how quantities like angular velocities or accelerations scale when time units change (minutes → seconds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and classify natural constants
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain tables of constants classified roughly as (i) mathematical, (ii) physical, (iii) astronomical, (iv) terrestrial, (v) organic, and (vi) social numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble important constants and their logarithms referred to common units; such collections (Babbage/Smithsonian-style) are valuable reference tools and facilitate cross-field calculations; recognize that some 'constants' (astronomical, terrestrial, organic, social) may vary and their laws of variation are themselves important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary objective of measurement: discover quantitative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal object of measurement is to discover general quantitative laws of nature; much preliminary labour involves accurate determination of dimensions of objects and numerical relations between forces and phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize precise, repeatable determination of numbers (e.g., coefficients, atomic weights, mechanical equivalents) because new constants exponentially expand the power of inference and prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary one condition at a time (ideal experimental principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the mathematical law connecting a quantitative cause to its effect, vary one condition at a time while keeping other conditions constant whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the guiding ideal for experimental design, though it is often only approximately achievable; attempt to isolate single-variable effects or use methods to approximate this condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomena are often compound and must be analysed
rubrics_metrics.description: An observed phenomenon is usually the sum, difference, product, or quotient of two or more different effects; these must be disentangled and separately measured before inductive treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and identify multiple contributing effects (examples: expansion of liquid plus expansion of containing glass; heat from carbon plus hydrogen combustion; conduction plus convection) and design experiments or calculations to separate them (subtraction, control measurements, compensated measurements).

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: one observation determines one quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: A single observation can render known only a single quantity; therefore, if several different quantitative effects enter an investigation, obtain at least as many distinct observations as quantities to be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan experiments as a series of operations arranged so that, guided by prior knowledge, simple mathematical processes distinguish separate quantities (use multiple measures, controls, and different configurations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the desired effect large relative to interfering effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If complete isolation is impossible, make the target effect as considerable as possible compared with interfering phenomena, and reduce the latter to a minimum, treating them as noxious errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design apparatus and procedures to maximize signal-to-interference ratio; remember that what is an 'error' in one experiment may be the phenomenon of interest in another, so document and, where possible, measure interfering effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek a special mode of experiment or opportunity of observation in which the error is non-existent or inappreciable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose experimental setups or conditions that eliminate the interfering cause (example implied: choosing a configuration where a secondary effect does not arise); avoidance is preferable when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Find observations when all interfering phenomena remain constant and only the subject of observation is alternately present and absent; the difference between observations gives the amount sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paired or differential measurements (example: differential barometer arrangement, or alternating sun/shade exposures for actinometry) to cancel out constant interfering influences and isolate the targeted effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the amount of the interfering effect by the best available mode and make a corresponding correction to the observed results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply calculated or empirically determined corrections (example: correcting barometric reading for thermometer-measured temperature-induced expansion) rather than ignoring known biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutralize the interfering cause by balancing it against an exactly equal and opposite cause of unknown amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use balancing or null methods (e.g., weighing tare, balancing forces) to produce a net-zero of the interference, thereby determining the unknown by equilibrium rather than direct measurement of large residuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct the experiment so that the interfering cause acts in opposite directions in alternate observations; the mean result is then free from that interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate orientations or signs of the interfering influence and average results to cancel symmetric biases (useful where exact compensation is difficult but reversal is possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combined experimental designs and controls to separate effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Where multiple small effects combine (e.g., radiative cooling vs absorbed solar heating), use control arrangements (shaded runs, closed vs open tubes, paired instruments) and mathematical subtraction to separate contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement controls parallel to the main measurement (example: a closed mercury tube to record temperature-only changes vs an open barometer), and apply subtraction/subtraction-plus-correction strategies to extract the desired quantity with higher accuracy.
